scenes.narration: About sixty percent. That is how much of America's daily supply of IV fluids came from a single factory in the mountains of North Carolina, according to the American Hospital Association.
In September twenty twenty-four, Hurricane Helene flooded that factory. Within days, hospitals across the country were told they could only order a fraction of the fluids they normally used.
So how does the richest country in the world end up depending on one building for a bag of salt water?

By the end of this video, you will know what happened inside that factory, how hospitals and regulators kept patients supplied, and why the economics of cheap medicine keep creating the same weak point.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Start with the product. An IV bag is mostly sterile water with a little salt or sugar. Hospitals use it for almost everything. To keep patients hydrated, to deliver drugs, during surgery, in the emergency room. It is one of the most common things in any hospital, and one of the cheapest.

The factory is called North Cove, near the town of Marion. It belongs to Baxter, a large medical company. Baxter calls it its largest manufacturing facility in the world, with more than two thousand five hundred employees. And it calls it the largest maker of IV and dialysis solutions in the United States.

The numbers are enormous. According to Baxter, the site produces more than a million IV solutions every single day. The hospital association put its share at about sixty percent of the IV solutions used in the country each day. Baxter itself never gave a percentage, so treat that figure as an estimate.

The building itself is huge. Baxter's fact sheet describes more than one point four million square feet, and more than five hundred million dollars invested in the site since twenty seventeen. It is not a small workshop that happened to flood. It is the heart of the system, built to be efficient.

And there are not many other makers. One competitor, ICU Medical, says in its annual report that its IV solutions compete in the U.S. with Baxter and B. Braun. Three companies, and one of them with one giant plant, carrying a large part of the load.

Let me draw the supply line. Here is one big factory. From it, trucks go out to distributors. From the distributors, to thousands of hospitals. Next to it, two smaller makers. Now notice the shape. Most of the arrows start in the same place.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: For years, that shape worked fine. Then, at the end of September twenty twenty-four, the rain came.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Hurricane Helene hit the southeast United States and dumped enormous amounts of rain on the mountains of western North Carolina. Rivers rose fast. At North Cove, Baxter said, heavy rain and the storm surge triggered a levee breach, and water got into the site.

By September twenty-ninth, Baxter announced that the site was closed for production. The bridges that led to the factory were damaged too. So the problem was not only the machines. Workers and trucks could not easily reach the building.

Making sterile fluids is not like making ordinary products. Every production line has to be cleaned, checked and proven safe before a single bag can be shipped. A flooded line cannot simply be dried out and switched back on.

Let me draw the flood. Here is the river. Here is the levee that holds it back. Here is the factory behind it. The water rises. The levee breaks. And one break in one place cuts off a large share of a whole country's supply.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Within days, hospitals across America felt it.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Baxter put its customers on allocation. That means each hospital could only order a set share of what it normally bought. At first, direct customers could get forty percent of their usual orders of the most needed fluids. For distributors, it was only ten percent. On October ninth, Baxter raised both to sixty percent, and set a goal of returning to ninety or one hundred percent for certain products by the end of the year.

Hospital pharmacists described the pressure. In a survey by their professional society in October, eighty-four percent of respondents said the shortage had a moderate or critical impact. A critical impact meant delaying or canceling treatments or procedures. And almost half of those who manage supplies said they had two weeks of fluids or less.

Regulators tried to stretch the supply. The FDA issued temporary guidance that let pharmacies prepare certain IV fluids themselves, something they normally could not do on this scale. Pharmacists, doctors and nurses had to decide, patient by patient, where each bag mattered most. For weeks, every single bag had to count, from the emergency room to the operating room.

Let me draw the allocation. Here is a normal order, one hundred bags. Under allocation, a direct customer gets sixty. A distributor, at first, got only ten. The gap between the order and the delivery is where hospitals had to improvise.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So the question became simple. Where could America find millions of extra bags, fast?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Regulators moved first. The Food and Drug Administration added several IV and dialysis solutions to its official shortage list. And it helped clear the temporary import of twenty-three different IV and dialysis fluids from five Baxter factories around the world.

Then came the planes. According to Baxter, by the end of twenty twenty-four, about two hundred airplanes had delivered product to the United States, nearly eighteen thousand tons of fluids, from plants in its global network. Water, flown across oceans, because the usual source was under repair.

The other makers pushed too. B. Braun said its plants in California and Florida would raise output by twenty percent. ICU Medical reported higher demand in the last months of the year. But neither could replace a plant of that size overnight.

Inside North Cove, the repair went line by line. Baxter restarted its first line about four and a half weeks after the flood, and released its first bags made after the storm on November twenty-first. It was the biggest one, about a quarter of the site's output. By late January twenty twenty-five, all ten lines were running again. On February seventeenth, Baxter said the site was back to its production levels from before the storm. That was less than five months after the flood.

The recovery was expensive. In its annual report, Baxter estimated that the storm cut its sales by one hundred and ten million dollars. It recorded three hundred and seventeen million dollars of cleanup, idle-plant and air freight costs, offset by two hundred and fifty-one million dollars from insurance.

Let me draw the recovery. Here is the flood, at the end of September. The first line, about a month later. All ten lines, at the end of January. Full output, in February. And in May twenty twenty-five, almost every product off allocation. Eight months, from flood to normal.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: The fluids came back. But the bigger question did not go away. Why was one building carrying so much in the first place?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The answer is in the price tag. The FDA studied drug shortages and listed the first root cause as a lack of incentives to make less profitable drugs. Of the shortage drugs it studied, sixty-three percent were sterile injectables. In the year before the shortage, the median price per unit was just eight dollars and seventy-three cents.

A government watchdog, the GAO, had found the same thing years earlier. Low profit margins had limited investment in factories for these cheap sterile products. When margins are thin, the cheapest way to make a product is in one huge plant, not in several smaller ones spread across the country.

And it had happened before. In twenty seventeen, Hurricane Maria disrupted saline production at a Baxter plant in Puerto Rico. Saline was already in short supply, and the storm made it worse. Then too, regulators let in fluids from Baxter plants abroad. The FDA described it in its own annual report on drug shortages for that year. Two storms, seven years apart, and the same lesson about the same kind of product.

Let me draw the trade-off. On one side, one big plant. Cheaper per bag, but one weak point. On the other, many smaller plants. More expensive, but if one floods, the others keep going. For a product sold for a few dollars, the market keeps choosing the first option.

scenes.narration: So how did one flooded factory run America short of IV fluids? Because the product is so cheap that nobody is paid to build a backup. The system is efficient on a normal day, and fragile on a bad one. The bags came back within months. The shape of the supply chain, with so many arrows starting in one place, is still the part to watch.
